title: Electrical Engineering Basics
summary: Learn the foundations of electrical engineering: charge, current, voltage and Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, power, energy and cost, AC, transformers and three-phase power, components and electronics, and electrical safety. All calculations were checked in code.
audience: School leavers, technicians, apprentices and anyone curious about electricity

body.p: Electrical engineering deals with generating, transmitting and using electricity, and with electronics and communication. Everything starts with four quantities.

list: Charge (Q), measured in coulombs, is carried by electrons.
Current (I), measured in amperes (A), is the rate of flow of charge.
Voltage (V), or potential difference, measured in volts, is the push that drives current; it is energy per unit charge.
Resistance (R), measured in ohms (Ω), opposes current.

body.p: For many conductors, V = I x R. A 12 V battery across a 4 Ω resistor drives a current of 12 / 4 = 3 A. Resistance depends on material, length, cross-section and temperature: longer, thinner wires have more resistance, which is why thick cables are needed for heavy currents.
Conductors (copper, aluminium) let current flow easily; insulators (plastic, rubber, glass) do not; semiconductors (silicon) sit in between and are the basis of electronics.

body.tip: Use the triangle V over I and R to remember Ohm's law: cover the quantity you want.

body.p: In a series circuit, components share one path. The same current flows through each, and resistances add: 4 Ω + 6 Ω = 10 Ω. With 12 V, the current is 12 / 10 = 1.2 A. If one component fails open, the whole circuit stops, like old strings of fairy lights.

In parallel, each component has its own path and the same voltage. The combined resistance is less than the smallest one: for 4 Ω and 6 Ω, R = (4 x 6) / (4 + 6) = 2.4 Ω. House wiring uses parallel circuits so each appliance gets full voltage and can be switched independently.

list: Current law: the total current into a junction equals the total current out.
Voltage law: around any closed loop, the voltage rises equal the voltage drops.
These two rules, with Ohm's law, let engineers analyse any circuit.

body.tip: Adding more parallel branches draws more total current from the supply, which is why overloading a socket with adaptors can overheat it.

body.p: Electrical power is P = V x I, measured in watts. A kettle drawing 5 A at 230 V uses 230 x 5 = 1150 W. Power can also be written P = I²R: a 3 A current through a 4 Ω resistor dissipates 3² x 4 = 36 W as heat.
Energy = power x time. Utilities bill in kilowatt-hours (kWh): 1 kWh is 1000 W for one hour. A 2 kW heater used for 3 hours uses 6 kWh; at R2.50 per kWh, that costs R15.

Efficiency is useful output divided by input. Losses usually appear as heat. When devices are connected in a chain, efficiencies multiply: a 90% efficient motor driven by a 95% efficient drive gives 0.9 x 0.95 = 85.5% overall.

list: LED lights use far less energy than incandescent bulbs for the same light.
Standby power adds up across many devices.
Heating and cooling appliances are usually the largest users in a home.

body.tip: Check appliance ratings in watts and estimate hours of use to find where your energy goes.

body.p: Mains electricity is alternating current (AC): the voltage reverses direction many times a second. Most of Africa uses 50 Hz, meaning 50 cycles per second. The 230 V quoted for mains is the root-mean-square (rms) value; the peak is about 325 V, since rms = peak / √2.

Transformers change AC voltage using two coils on an iron core. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio. Stepping 230 V down to 12 V needs a turns ratio of about 230 / 12 = 19.17 : 1. Power stations step voltage up to hundreds of kilovolts for transmission, because at higher voltage the same power needs less current, so less energy is lost as heat (losses go with I²R).

Industry uses three-phase supplies, which deliver power smoothly and run motors efficiently. Power is P = √3 x V x I x power factor: 400 V, 10 A and a power factor of 0.85 give about 1.732 x 400 x 10 x 0.85 = 5889 W.

body.tip: The grid must balance supply and demand every second; load shedding happens when generation cannot meet demand.

list: Resistors limit current and divide voltage.
Capacitors store energy in an electric field: E = ½CV². A 100 μF capacitor at 12 V stores 0.5 x 0.0001 x 144 = 0.0072 J. They smooth power supplies and block DC.
Inductors store energy in a magnetic field and resist changes in current.
Diodes let current flow one way; rectifiers use them to turn AC into DC. LEDs are diodes that emit light.
Transistors act as switches and amplifiers and are the building blocks of computer chips.
Integrated circuits pack millions or billions of transistors onto one chip.

body.p: Analogue signals vary smoothly; digital signals use two levels, 0 and 1. Microcontrollers such as those on Arduino boards read sensors and control motors and lights, and are widely used in learning, prototyping and products such as smart meters and solar charge controllers.

body.tip: A multimeter that measures voltage, current and resistance is the most useful tool for any electrical learner.

body.p: Electricity can kill. Currents of a few tens of milliamps through the body can stop the heart. Wet skin lowers body resistance and greatly increases danger.

list: Isolate and lock off circuits before working on them, and test that they are dead with a proven tester.
Earthing gives fault current a safe path, so protective devices operate.
Circuit breakers and fuses protect cables from overcurrent; residual current devices (RCDs or earth-leakage units) trip at around 30 mA to protect people.
Never bypass protection or use damaged cables.
Only qualified, registered electricians should do fixed wiring work.

body.p: Electrical engineers and technicians work in power generation and utilities, renewable energy, mining, manufacturing, telecommunications, electronics and building services. Routes include degrees, diplomas and trade apprenticeships leading to registration as an electrician.

body.tip: Treat every circuit as live until you have proved it dead.
